archetype.name: Point Guard (scramble-capable)
archetype.definition: A rhythm distributor who completes a high share of short, horizontal throws to Olave, Vele and Juwan Johnson, does his best work when he pushes the ball past ten yards, and uses scrambles rather than designed runs as his release valve.

report.headline: Accurate, productive past ten yards, but screens, third downs and fumbles cap him
report.take:
Tyler Shough is a second-year starter who has taken every snap that mattered for the Saints this season, and his line reads better in volume than in efficiency. He ranks 14th in passing yards per game (241.4) and 14th in PPR points, completes 66.8% (11th, 4.2 points over the qualifier average), yet averages just 6.34 yards per attempt (37th) and 0.016 EPA per dropback (27th). That is still above the league average, but it is the profile of a quarterback who moves the chains on volume more than he drives the ball. His intended air yards sit at 7.43 and his throws land 1.46 yards short of the sticks on average.

The split that explains him is depth. On throws under ten air yards he is at 0.035 EPA per attempt; on throws of ten-plus he is at 0.292, with the intermediate band (0.351 on 61 attempts) and the middle of the field (0.316) his best work. What drags the short game down is the screen and swing layer: 60 throws behind the line have cost -20.7 EPA, which wipes out most of what his 0-9 yard throws add. The target tree tells the same story. Olave, Vele and Johnson all clear 0.27 EPA per target, while Kamara (0.006) and Bryce Lance (-9.3 EPA total) are where possessions go to die. He has become more aggressive than as a rookie (15.74% tight-window throws against 12.8%) and his bad-throw rate fell 1.9 points. Still, his yards per attempt is down 0.95 and his CPOE down 2. More of his work is being funneled into low-value touches.

The numbers hide two things that cut opposite ways. His touchdown line leans on the red zone: 13 of his 15 passing scores came there, on an 11.3 CPOE that is unlikely to hold. His touchdown rate over the last three games has already dropped to 2.8%. On the other side, his pocket work has quietly improved. His pressure-to-sack rate is 27.8% against 41.9% as a rookie, and his 19 scrambles are worth 0.468 EPA apiece with nine first downs. The real flaws are ball security and third down. His four lost fumbles are the most among 54 qualifiers, with nine fumbles charted as turnover-worthy. Third downs run at -0.125 EPA with 11 sacks, because he is usually facing 7.7 yards to go in an offense that won't run.

Where it heads depends on a line that just lost three starters. Taliese Fuaga and Erik McCoy, both near every-snap players, are out, and Asim Richards is out for multiple weeks. His sack rate over the last three games has already climbed to 8.5%. With a 28th-ranked rushing attack and a 23rd-ranked defense behind him, the Saints will keep throwing, so the volume is safe. The efficiency is not.

strengths.title: Wins when he throws past ten
strengths.body: His throws of ten-plus air yards return 0.292 EPA, with the intermediate range and the middle of the field doing the heavy lifting. That comes from reading leverage and hitting Olave and Vele in windows rather than from arm talent alone. It has held across nine games, so it is a real skill. The open question is whether Kellen Moore calls enough of it.

strengths.title: Scrambles pay, sacks shrinking
strengths.body: He scrambles on 4.9% of dropbacks at 0.468 EPA per scramble. His pressure-to-sack rate has fallen from 41.9% as a rookie to 27.8%, so he now escapes with purpose instead of holding the ball. That is year-two growth with a clear cause, and it should travel. A depleted line will test it, though.

strengths.title: Efficient to his top three
strengths.body: Olave (0.337 EPA per target on 87 targets), Vele and Juwan Johnson all produce at a high level. When the ball goes to them, the offense works. The structure is sound; the inefficiency comes from where else the ball goes.

concerns.title: Worst ball security among qualifiers
concerns.body: His four lost fumbles rank 54th of 54, and nine fumbles were charted as turnover-worthy. Some fumble recovery is luck, but nine loose balls point to a habit: carrying the ball loosely when extending plays and taking hits. With his line thinning out, the exposure goes up, not down.

concerns.title: Horizontal offense sinks third down
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have cost -20.7 EPA, and his average throw lands short of the sticks. That combination shows up on third down: -0.125 EPA with 11 sacks, facing 7.7 yards to go. Part of this is scheme and a rushing game that leaves him in long yardage. Part is his own preference for the easy completion.

concerns.title: Three line starters now out
concerns.body: Fuaga at tackle and McCoy at center are both out, and Richards is sidelined for multiple weeks after the Carolina loss. His sack rate over the last three games is already 2.2 points above his season mark. Shotgun dropbacks, where most of his sacks come, will get harder to operate behind backups.

trend.note: His game EPA has ranged from +9.5 against Baltimore to -9.4 against Minnesota. The last three went +8.3, -1.4 and -3.2, with accuracy steadier (last-three CPOE 1.4) but sacks and the touchdown rate moving the wrong way.

nextGame.headline: Bears choke the short game behind a patched Saints line
nextGame.body:
Chicago is built to take away exactly what Shough leans on. The Bears allow -0.154 EPA on short throws, second-best in the league, and get home at the third-best sack rate. Their leak is deep: 1.133 EPA on deep throws ranks dead last. That means the efficient path runs through the ten-plus throws he already does well, not the screens and checkdowns that fill his volume. As an 11.5-point underdog (+470), the Saints should be throwing a lot. That supports his yardage, though he has been below average when trailing by nine or more.

Availability tilts it further. Without Fuaga, McCoy and Richards, the Saints are asking backups to hold up against a top-three sack defense. That raises both his sack and fumble exposure and shortens the time he needs for intermediate and deep drops. On the Bears side, cornerback Malik Muhammad II was listed out and Tyrique Stevenson questionable with a hand injury, as of reports from Nov. 9. If either sits, the secondary that already gives up big plays gets thinner, which helps Olave. The early forecast calls for 16 mph wind with 26 mph gusts outdoors, though it is five days out. If that holds, it would cut into the very deep shots Chicago allows.

keyMatchups.title: Short-game wall, deep-ball sieve
keyMatchups.body: Chicago ranks second against short throws and last against deep ones. His 0.198 EPA on 20-plus yard throws comes on a 35.9% completion rate. The opportunity is there, but it depends on time and on Moore calling it.

keyMatchups.title: Bears rush vs backup line
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's sack rate ranks third. Shough has been sacked on 8.5% of dropbacks over his last three games, before losing three line starters. Expect more scrambles, more hits and more loose-ball risk.

keyMatchups.title: Big underdog in possible wind
keyMatchups.body: The spread points to a trailing game script that props up attempts. His EPA when trailing by nine-plus is negative, though, and gusty conditions would hurt the deep throws Chicago concedes. Volume should be fine; efficiency is the worry.

nextGame.watch: Whether Moore keeps calling intermediate and deep shots to Olave against a thin Bears secondary, or retreats to screens that Chicago's short-throw defense swallows.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume holds. New Orleans passes more than expected (10th), can't run the ball (28th in rush EPA) and fields a 23rd-ranked defense that keeps games open, so 35-plus attempts a week is the baseline. Expect yardage roughly in line with his 241.4 per game, settling into a 205-255 range while the line is patched. The touchdown rate is the likeliest thing to cool: 13 of his 15 passing scores came on red-zone accuracy far above expectation, and the last three games already show it fading toward 1.0-1.6 per game. His scramble value and improved sack avoidance are real, but they will be stress-tested by backups up front, with something like 2.3-3.5 sacks a game while Richards is out.

The upside case is simple: Fuaga and McCoy return soon, as their estimated dates suggest, and the offense shifts weight from behind-the-line throws to the ten-plus routes where he produces. The downside case is the one already forming: rising sacks, more fumbles and stalled third downs, with his EPA sliding back toward league average or below. Fumbles are the wild card; recovery luck can swing, but nine turnover-worthy fumbles say the risk is his.
swingFactors: Return timing of Fuaga and McCoy
Share of throws at ten-plus air yards vs. behind the line

confidence.note: Nine starts give a clear profile, but three line starters out makes the next few weeks hard to read.
